name: Archery
tagline: Stillness at 70 meters — the bow, the breath, and a ten the size of an apple.
overview: Archery is precision shooting with a bow: arrows loosed at target faces scored in rings from 10 (gold, with the ten ring itself spanning 12.2 cm at 70 m Olympic distance) down to 1. The Olympic discipline is the recurve bow at 70 meters, shot in set-based match play; the compound bow (cams, sights, releases) governs the indoor and World Games branches; barebow is tradition's growing purist division.

A hunting and warfare tool for millennia, archery became organized sport in 19th-century Britain (the Grand National Archery Society, 1844, York rounds) and appeared at the 1900 Paris Olympics before settling into the modern program from Munich 1972. South Korea built the sport's greatest dynasty — the women's team has lost one Olympic gold since 1984 — while World Archery's circuit now spans recurve, compound, barebow, indoor, field, 3D, and ski archery.

Newcomers should expect archery to be a mental sport wearing a technical costume: the shot sequence (stance, nock, set, setup, draw, anchor, aim, release, follow-through) is trained as one repeatable ritual, and scoring follows the archer's calm more than their strength. Start with a club's beginner course and rental gear: recurve first, and let form precede equipment.

skills: Shot sequence & form
One repeatable ritual: stance, set, setup, draw, anchor, expansion, release, follow-through — the sport's entire technical bible.
Blank-bale shooting (5 m, no target) to groove sequence; form checks in the mirror monthly; one element consciously trained per session.
Aiming & sight discipline
The sight floats; the archer holds through the float — aiming is timing, not snapping.
Float-acceptance shooting (shoot within 3 seconds of settling); sight marks recorded per distance; clicker discipline for recurve.
Release & follow-through
A surprise release with the back muscles (not fingers deciding), and a motionless follow-through that proves it.
Resistance-band release training daily; back-tension drills (SPT — specific physical training sets); video of the release finger monthly.
Scoring under pressure
Set play rewards clutch execution: training the last arrow of a tied set like a heartbeat skill.
Pressure simulations (shooting for consequences with training partners); timed ends (20 s left, one arrow, hit to win); heart-rate training.
Equipment tuning
Bow tuning, arrow spine matching, and sight calibration — the sport's engineering half.
Bare-shaft and walk-back tuning per setup change; arrow spine and weight matching logged; a tuning notebook kept forever.
Physical conditioning
Draw-specific strength (SPT) and posture endurance: a 70 m round is a standing marathon of stillness.
SPT draw-holds (3×10 at anchor); band training daily; core and shoulder stability 2× weekly; cardio for steady heart rate.
rules: Olympic match play: 3-arrow sets (individual), first to 6 set points wins (2 per set, 1 for tie); shoot-offs by closest-to-center single arrow.
Ranking rounds: 72 arrows at 70 m recurve (122 cm face); compound 50 m trispot; indoor 18 m standard 60 arrows.
Time limits: 20 seconds per arrow (individual match play ends of 4 minutes; end timing by format); equipment failures policed.
Scoring: arrow value by ring cut (line-cutters score the higher value); X-ring (inner ten) breaks ties; contested arrows called before pulling.

Equipment rules: recurve division limits (no sights' magnification, finger release required); compound allows sights, levels, and mechanical releases within draw-weight caps; arrows' diameter limits apply.
Team events: three archers, alternating ends (2 arrows each per end, per format), 24-arrow matches; mixed team one man and one woman.
Etiquette and safety: the whistle system (2 to shoot, 3 to retrieve), no dry-firing, and line discipline — archery's safety record depends on it.

Arrows
Carbon arrows cut and fletched to your setup; a dozen matched ($60-200); field points for targets.
Protection & accessories
Finger tab or glove, armguard, chest guard, quiver, and a bow stand ($80-150 together).
Targets
Straw or foam bosses with target faces ($100-400 club-shared); portable bag targets for home practice.
training: Volume with structure: 3-5 sessions weekly, 60-150 arrows each, every arrow shot with full sequence intent.
SPT (specific physical training): draw-holds, expansion drills, and interval draw work — archery's gym.
Mental training is technical training: breathing routines, shot-timing discipline, and refocus rituals trained on every practice arrow.

name: Shooting Sport
tagline: Breath held, trigger honored — millimeters and mindset at ten or fifty meters.
overview: Shooting sport divides into precision events — rifle and pistol fired at paper or electronic targets from 10 to 50 meters — and clay target shotgun disciplines (trap, skeet, sporting), where moving targets shatter into dust. The Olympic program spans fifteen events from the 10 m air rifle (whose smallest scoring ring, the decimal-era inner ten, is 0.5 mm) to the trench of Olympic trap, and the sport's essence is identical across all: stillness, sight alignment, and a trigger released by surprise.

Shooting appeared at the first modern Olympics in 1896; the ISSF (founded 1907) governs the precision disciplines while the FITASC world governs sporting clays. The sport's icons are its obsessives: shooters like Abhinav Bindra (India's first individual Olympic gold) and Kim Rhode (six Games, six medals) built careers on process — and the women's 10 m air rifle final now crowns the Games' first gold of every Olympiad.

Newcomers should begin with supervised club instruction — safety is the sport's first curriculum and permanent culture — starting with 10 m air rifle or pistol, the quietest and most technical of entries. Precision shooting rewards dry-fire discipline (training without ammunition) as much as live rounds, and the sport's aging curve is famously kind: Olympians compete from teens to fifties.

Mental routine & finals craft

Routine scripting and rehearsal; finals simulations with noise and elimination stakes; refocus routines after bad shots.
rules: Universal safety law: muzzle discipline, finger off trigger until on target, actions open, and range commands absolute — every range's first language.

name: Golf
tagline: A walk measured in strokes — the most mentally exposed sport ever invented.
overview: Golf is played by striking a ball from a tee into a hole in as few strokes as possible, across 18-hole courses of tees, fairways, hazards, and greens — a round the professional completes in 70ish strokes and the amateur spends four hours negotiating with hope. It is the only major sport where the playing field changes at every venue, the opponent is the course and your own mind, and the scorecard's arithmetic admits no interpretation.

Born on Scotland's linksland by the 15th century (James II briefly banned it as an archery distraction), golf grew through the Royal & Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews (1754) and The Open Championship (1860) into a global game of four majors, the Ryder Cup's nationalism, and a handicap system that lets a beginner compete honestly against a professional. The modern era runs from Bobby Jones' Grand Slam through Nicklaus' eighteen majors, Tiger Woods' twenty-first-century transformation of the sport's athleticism and audience, and the LIV-versus-PGA restructuring of the professional landscape.

Newcomers should learn the short game first — putting and chipping decide amateur scores — and take a handful of lessons before grooving a swing: golf punishes self-taught habits for decades. The handicap system is the sport's welcoming genius: track your scores, and every course on Earth will tell you exactly how you stand.

Impact-bag and divot drills; slow-motion video of low-point control; short swings (9-to-3) struck purely before full swings.

Grip, posture, takeaway, backswing turn, transition, sequence (hips-then-torso-then-arms), release, finish: one repeatable motion.
Lesson series with a professional (5 lessons beat 50 tips); mirror and video work; single-thought rehearsals under pressure.

Routine scripting (45-75 seconds) rehearsed identically; post-shot refocus rituals; breathing between shots; scorecard amnesia.
rules: The Rules of Golf (R&A/USGA, updated quadrennially): play the ball as it lies, the course as you find it, and if you cannot do either, do what is fair — the code's soul.

Stroke limits and pace: ready golf encouraged; maximum-score formats (double par or net double bogey caps) protect pace in handicap play.
Equipment conformity: club and ball lists (model-local rules allow conforming-ball conditions), the 14-club maximum, and distance-measuring devices by local rule.
Handicap system (WHS — the World Handicap System 2020): course rating + slope + your scoring record produce a portable index; caps and exceptional-score adjustments keep it honest.
Etiquette as law: repairing the course, pace of play, and safety — the sport's self-policing culture.

name: Darts
tagline: Treble twenty, double out — the pub game that became a world television sport.
overview: Darts is thrown at a circular board divided into 20 numbered segments, doubles and trebles rings, and a bullseye — scored 1 to 60 per dart (treble 20) with matches raced from 501 to exactly zero, finishing on a double. The standard game's genius is the checkout arithmetic: players subtract to leave doubles (40, 32, 16, and so on), and the drama of a nine-dart perfect leg or a missed double for a world title has made darts one of television's most-watched sports events in Britain and the Netherlands.

Born as a pub pastime (the 'trebles' board standardizing in the 1920s), the sport organized professionally in the 1970s, split into the BDO and PDC (1992-94 era), and the PDC era built the sport we know: Alexandra Palace's world championship filling 90,000+ seats across the fortnight, the Premier League's arena tour, and prize funds past £2.5 million at worlds. The 2020s added the sport's youngest superstars — Luke Littler reaching the world final at sixteen (2024) — and a global surge in board sales.

Newcomers should know the sport's ladder is genuinely open: a board, a tape measure (the oche at 7 ft 9¼ in, the bull at 5 ft 8 in), and practice. Grouping before scoring: throw at the treble 20 bed until three darts sit together, then learn the checkouts (170 is the maximum finish) — darts is arithmetic performed with a steady hand.

Throwing distance

The standard game
501, straight in, double out: legs and sets in match play; 301 variants for casual play
Governing bodies

Maximum finish
170 (T20-T20-Bull) — the biggest checkout; nine-dart legs are the perfect 501 (two 180s plus a 141 finish)
Broadcast era

name: Snooker
tagline: The green baize's long game — 147 points of silence and geometry.
overview: Snooker is played on a 12×6 ft table with 15 reds and six colours: players pot reds (1 point) alternating with colours (yellow 2 through black 7), clearing the reds then the colours in order, scoring more points than the opponent per frame. It is cue sport's chess — position play (cue-ball control for the next shot) matters more than potting, and safety battles (returning the cue ball to safety behind baulk colours) can last longer than some nations' constitutions.

Invented around 1875 by British officers in Jabalpur, India (Sir Neville Chamberlain among them, naming novice cadets 'snookers'), the sport professionalized through Joe Davis' dominance (1927-1946) and exploded in the television era — 'pot black' color broadcasts, the Crucible Theatre's world championship since 1977, and the 1985 final's 18.6 million midnight viewers. The modern game runs the rhythm of triple-crown majors and a Chinese circuit's rise, with Ronnie O'Sullivan's seven world titles and fifteen maximum breaks crowning the sport's greatest natural gift.

Newcomers should build the fundamentals in order: a straight delivery (cueing along the line), then position play (natural angle followed by spin: screw, side, stun-run-through), then the tactical vocabulary (snookers, escapes, and safety exchanges). The 147 maximum break — fifteen reds with blacks, then all six colours — remains sport's most exclusive perfect score, achieved professionally only a couple dozen times, a handful per decade.

name: Pool (Billiards)
tagline: Eight ball, nine ball, one table — the world's bar-room cue sport with a pro soul.
overview: Pool is the family of cue games played on seven-to-nine-foot tables with sixteen balls: eight-ball (solids versus stripes, finish on the 8), nine-ball (the rotation game — pot the 9 legally at any time to win), ten-ball, straight pool, and the discipline-specific variants. Where snooker rewards sustained break-building, pool rewards shot-making density and tactical closure — the games are shorter, the pockets less forgiving relative to ball size than they look, and a single visit can decide a rack.

The game evolved from European billiards on American tables through the 1800s (the name from French poële, the pocket-game family), professionalized through the hustling era and the color-money 1970s (the Hustler's cultural shadow), and now runs a world structure under the WPA with the Matchroom-era professional renaissance: the Mosconi Cup's USA-versus-Europe team war, the World Pool Championship, and the US Open's heritage coats.

Newcomers should master the fundamentals that transfer from snooker (delivery, position) on the smaller canvas, then learn pool's specific crafts: the break (nine-ball's wings — a controlled weapon of its own), safeties with one-cushion kick and bank systems, and pattern play in eight-ball (clearing your group with the 8 in mind). The table's social availability — every bar, every club — makes pool the most played cue sport on Earth.

name: Tenpin Bowling
tagline: Twelve strikes away from perfection — the 300 game and the oil pattern's quiet science.
overview: Tenpin bowling rolls a ball down a 60-foot lane to topple ten pins: a game is ten frames, strikes (all ten on the first ball) and spares compound scoring, and perfection is the 300 game — twelve consecutive strikes. Under the sport's friendly lounge exterior runs a genuinely technical discipline: lane oil patterns (invisible, changing with every ball thrown) dictate how the ball hooks, and elite bowlers read oil migration and adjust lines frame by frame.

The American Bowling Congress standardized the sport in 1895 (New York, with roots in Dutch-German kegeln), the automatic pinsetter (1940s-50s) created the modern mass leisure era, and the Professional Bowlers Association (founded 1958) built the sport's television legacy — Earl Anthony's era to today's two-handed revolution. Globally, the WB (World Bowling) family counts 100+ federations, with bowling long-listed repeatedly for Olympic recognition.

Newcomers should start with house-ball basics (a fitted ball changes everything — buy your own early), learn the four-step approach and a straight, consistent release, then discover the sport's real depth: hook bowling with a fingertip drill, adjusting to lane conditions, and spare shooting — the amateur scoring separator. A perfect 300 remains one of sport's most treasured certificates: tens of thousands are bowled yearly, and each one is somebody's best day ever.

name: Disc Golf
tagline: Golf's rebellion — chains instead of cups, flight numbers instead of yardages.
overview: Disc golf is played like ball golf: throw from a tee toward a basket (an elevated pole with hanging chains that catch the disc), count strokes to hole out, lowest score wins. Courses run through parks and woods worldwide, holes from 60 to 300 meters, and the equipment vocabulary is flight numbers — speed, glide, turn, and fade — describing how each of a dozen possible discs flies.

Invented informally in the 1960s (Frisbee culture's kids) and formalized by 'Steady' Ed Headrick — who patented the basket (1975, the Disc Pole Hole) and founded the PDGA (1976) — the sport has grown explosively: 10,000+ courses worldwide, a professional tour with video coverage and six-figure career earnings, and a pandemic-era participation surge that made it one of the fastest-growing outdoor activities on record.

Newcomers need almost nothing: three discs (a putter, a midrange, a fairway driver) and a public course. The technique ladder runs putter → midrange → driver (control before distance), and the game's chess is shot shaping: hyzers and anhyzers, flex shots and rollers chosen against wind and trees, exactly as a golfer chooses draws and fades. Putting to the chains — the sound is addictive — is where rounds are decided.

name: Pétanque
tagline: Steel balls, a wooden jack, and the Mediterranean art of pointing and shooting.
overview: Pétanque is played by throwing hollow steel boules toward a small wooden jack (the cochonnet, or 'little pig'): teams of one, two, or three players compete to place their boules closest, with points scored per boule nearer than the opponent's best. The game's two crafts are pointing (landing and rolling boules with precision) and shooting (the direct strike that removes an opponent's boule — tir, the thunderclap of the sport).

Born in 1910 at La Ciotat, Provence (the name from pes tanats — feet planted together, a stationary evolution of the running jeu provençal adapted to suit an elder champion who could no longer run), pétanque ranks among France's most-played sports and is the world's great square-and-café game: the FIPJP (founded 1958) counts 600,000+ licensed players across 100+ federations, with world championships and a professional-adjacent elite of shooting specialists.

Newcomers need boules (by hand size and playing style), a jack, and any patch of gravel: the sport's terrain is deliberately variable — planes, slopes, and stones are the course's design. Learn pointing before shooting (the carreau — a shot that replaces the struck boule exactly — is the sharpshooter's holy grail), and embrace the rhythm: measure, argue, agree, and throw again.

rules: Play from a circle (50 cm, drawn or fixed): both feet on the ground inside the circle until the boule lands.
The jack thrown 6-10 m (by category rules); a dead jack (out of the terrain's boundaries) leads to an award or continuation by the rules of the end's state.
Scoring: after all boules are thrown, the team with the closest boule scores one point per boule closer than the opponent's best; games to 13.
Order of play: the team NOT holding the point throws until it holds the point or runs out of boules.
Boules out of the terrain are dead; boules moved by other boules' action stand as they lie (with prescribed remedies for moved jacks and obstacles).
Shooting legality: a shooting boule must land within a set radius of the target (50 cm at elite rules); accidental or deliberate short throws are faults.
